nameStory: The Labyrinth Orbweaver gets its mysterious name from its unique web-building behavior. Unlike other orbweavers that create simple circular webs, this spider constructs a complex maze-like structure with additional retreat chambers and tangled barrier webs surrounding the main orb. It's like finding a spider's secret fortress hidden in the vegetation!
description: The Labyrinth Orbweaver is a small, round-bodied spider with a distinctive bulbous abdomen and surprisingly thin legs. Females reach about 5mm in body length with legs spanning nearly 20mm when extended. Their brown or gray bodies feature striking white markings on a dark abdomen, while their legs show alternating bands of pale and dark brown that create a zebra-striped appearance.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for the telltale maze-like web structure with a central orb surrounded by tangled retreat areas and barrier threads - it feels more substantial and complex than typical circular orbweaver webs

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Notice the dramatically bulbous, round abdomen paired with surprisingly thin, delicate legs that seem almost too skinny for the chunky body

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Spot the white pattern standing out against the dark abdomen, plus look for the distinctive yellow stripe running down the center of the dark brown underside

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: The eye region appears notably lighter in color than the rest of the brown or gray head area, creating a pale 'face mask' effect

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females measure about 5mm in body length while males are slightly smaller - think roughly the size of a small pea with thin legs extended

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found sitting in their complex web retreats rather than hanging in the center of the orb like most orbweavers

habitat: Labyrinth Orbweavers prefer shrubby areas, forest edges, and gardens where they can anchor their complex webs between multiple branches or stems. They're often found in areas with dense vegetation that provides good support for their elaborate web structures. Look for them in both natural woodland borders and cultivated landscapes with plenty of branching plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing and web-building activity increases as temperatures warm and prey becomes more abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most elaborate and spiders are actively hunting. This is the best time to observe their distinctive labyrinthine web structures.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced before adults die off with the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Only egg sacs survive the winter, usually hidden in protected locations near where the webs were built.

funFact: The Labyrinth Orbweaver is basically an architect among spiders - it builds what amounts to a spider apartment complex, with a main circular web for catching prey plus separate retreat rooms, escape tunnels, and barrier walls all integrated into one amazing structure!
confusionNotes: Most other small orbweavers build simple circular webs and sit in the center waiting for prey, making the Labyrinth Orbweaver's complex maze-web the easiest way to distinguish it. Memory trick: 'Labyrinth' in the name equals 'labyrinth' web structure.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an orbweaver, this spider's web is much more than just an orb - the name refers to its family membership rather than describing its actual web architecture. The 'labyrinth' part of its name is the key descriptor that sets it apart from its simpler web-building relatives.
compareHints: Since this is the only Metepeira species in New England, compare it to other small orbweavers in the Araneidae family by focusing on the web structure first. While other orbweavers like the Common Garden Spider build clean, geometric orb webs, the Labyrinth Orbweaver's composite web with retreat areas and barrier threads is unmistakable. The light eye region and yellow sternum stripe also help distinguish it from similar-sized relatives.
